lead: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave: gas layers vibrate along the direction of travel, and ears read its frequency and intensity. Acoustics turns that wave into engineering numbers: pressure amplitude, speed, intensity, decibel level and room absorption. These numbers decide whether a lecture hall is clear, a cinema is comfortable, or a factory is dangerously loud. The same ideas size echo cancelling, noise barriers and ultrasound links. The pressure-wave model, decibel scale and Sabine’s room formula tie them together.
prereq: You need: wave equation and wave energy and intensity.

blocks.text: Sound in a gas is a longitudinal wave: gas layers move back and forth along the direction of travel. The wave carries a pressure change p(x,t) = P₀ sin(kx − ωt). P₀ is pressure amplitude in pascal (Pa); k = 2π/λ is angular wavenumber in rad/m; ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s; t is time in s. Intensity I is energy crossing unit area per second, in W/m². For a plane wave, I = P₀²/(2ρv). ρ is gas density in kg/m³; v is speed in m/s. Speed in air follows v = √(γRT/M). γ is the ratio of specific heats (dimensionless); R = 8.314 J/(mol K); T is absolute temperature in K; M is molar mass in kg/mol. At 293 K, air with γ = 1.40 and M = 0.029 kg/mol gives about 343 m/s. The formula assumes a plane wave in a uniform gas. Only a few universities teach acoustics at this depth.

Human hearing spans a huge intensity range, so we use a logarithmic scale. Sound level is L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) dB. I is intensity in W/m²; I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² is the reference at 1 kHz, near the hearing threshold. A change of 10 dB means ten times the intensity; 20 dB means one hundred times. Because intensity goes as pressure squared, L = 20 log₁₀(P₀/P₀,ref) for pressure in the same medium. The reference pressure in air is usually P₀,ref = 20 μPa. Ordinary talk is about 60 dB; a whisper about 30 dB; a loud concert can reach 110 dB. At 120 dB sound is near pain. Doubling distance from a point source in free space lowers intensity by factor 4, about 6 dB. A 3 dB rise is about twice the intensity. Use 10 log for intensity and 20 log for pressure. The decibel itself is dimensionless.

Inside a hall, sound reflects from walls, floor and ceiling. A hard surface returns most energy and creates echoes; a soft surface absorbs. The absorption coefficient α (dimensionless) is the fraction of incident energy absorbed. Effective absorption is A = Σ αᵢ Sᵢ, measured in m² sabins. Sᵢ is surface area in m². Sabine’s reverberation time T₆₀ is the time for sound to fall by 60 dB after the source stops: T₆₀ = 0.161 V/A. V is room volume in m³; A is total absorption in m² sabins. The constant 0.161 has unit s/m. Large V or small A gives long reverberation. Echo is a distinct reflected sound heard after about 0.1 s; reverberation is many overlapping reflections. Curtains, carpets and acoustic panels raise A and shorten T₆₀. A room with too long T₆₀ smears speech. A room with too short T₆₀ feels dead.

figure.caption: Sound level against intensity ratio. A tenfold rise in intensity adds 10 dB, so 10⁻¹² W/m² gives 0 dB and 1 W/m² gives 120 dB.

spec.aria: A logarithmic curve from 0 dB at the hearing threshold to 120 dB at the pain threshold.

examples.question: A hall has volume V = 500 m³ and total absorption A = 50 m² sabins. Find its reverberation time. Also find the sound level of intensity I = 10⁻⁵ W/m².
steps: For sound level, use I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m². Ratio I/I₀ = 10⁻⁵/10⁻¹² = 10⁷.
L = 10 log₁₀(10⁷) = 10 × 7 = 70 dB. With one decimal, 70.0 dB.
examples.check:
import math
V = 500.0
A = 50.0
T60 = 0.161 * V / A
I = 1e-5
I0 = 1e-12
L = 10 * math.log10(I / I0)
print(f"{T60:.2f}")
print(f"{L:.1f}")

traps: Using 20 log₁₀ for intensity level; 20 log₁₀ belongs to pressure or amplitude ratio.
Putting floor area in A; Sabine’s A is total absorption ΣαS, not room area.
Using T in °C in v = √(γRT/M); T must be kelvin.
Taking M in g/mol; use kg/mol so R = 8.314 J/(mol K) matches.
Using I₀ = 10⁻⁶ W/m²; the standard air reference is 10⁻¹² W/m².

quiz.q: State the reference intensity I₀ for sound level in air.
Why is sound level defined on a logarithmic scale?
quiz.a: The hearing range is huge; a logarithm compresses large intensity ratios into small numbers.

quiz.q: An intensity is 10⁻⁸ W/m². Find its sound level.
A room’s volume doubles while total absorption stays the same. What happens to T₆₀?
quiz.a: T₆₀ = 0.161 V/A is proportional to V, so it doubles. Reverberation becomes longer.

quiz.q: Estimate the speed of sound in air at T = 300 K with γ = 1.40 and M = 0.029 kg/mol.
Give one difference between an echo and reverberation.
quiz.a: An echo is a distinct reflection heard after a delay; reverberation is many overlapping reflections that decay gradually.

quiz.q: Why does a carpet lower a room’s reverberation time?
quiz.a: The carpet raises total absorption A, so T₆₀ = 0.161 V/A becomes smaller.

beyond: Not for the exam. Architectural acoustics uses these numbers to design auditoria, open offices and noise barriers. In research, room impulse responses and absorption coefficients are measured, not guessed. Ultrasound imaging and sonar reuse the same pressure-wave equations at higher frequency. Search next for Sabine reverberation time, sound absorption coefficient, A-weighted decibel and room impulse response.
